solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Quiet in stomach, after upset at first: result! (6)

indicatorNotes.at first: 'at first' asks for only what comes first in 'upset', its opening letter
indicatorNotes.in: 'in stomach' places the quiet SH inside the POT, as food sits in a belly

blocks.note: a pot, as in pot belly
sh! = be quiet, placed inside POT

annotation.surface: Someone with a queasy stomach settling down after an upset, with a cheerful exclamation of relief.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon before 'result' is the break: everything ahead of it is wordplay. 'After' puts U in front of the stuffed pot.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the eventual outcome of a chain of events.

entries.clue: Source of cheese roll initially eaten by parents (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: 'initially' means at the start, so only the first letter of 'roll' is used
indicatorNotes.eaten by: food eaten by someone ends up inside them, so R goes inside PA MA

blocks.note: PA and MA, the two parents
first letter of roll, placed between PA and MA

annotation.surface: A family meal where a cheese roll gets polished off by the grown-ups.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pairs cheese with a roll so the solver pictures a sandwich; the roll is only there for its R.
annotation.definitionFit: Parma in northern Italy gives Parmesan (Parmigiano) its name.

entries.clue: Well-off people storing equipment: number show anxiety (4,7)

indicatorNotes.storing: to store something is to keep it inside, so HAVES keeps KIT and TEN within it

blocks.note: the haves, as against the have-nots
any number will do; here ten, also inside HAVES

annotation.surface: Rich people hoarding their gear, with a count that makes someone nervous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number' can be any number at all, so let the crossing letters choose it. To have kittens is British slang for being in a state of panic.
annotation.definitionFit: A British idiom for getting extremely agitated, as a cat might in labour.

entries.clue: In addition, husband pocketing pounds for roadside kiosk (8)

indicatorNotes.pocketing: to pocket something is to put it inside, so TO BOOT takes L inside it

blocks.note: to boot = as well, in addition
L = pounds sterling (£), placed after TO
H = husband, added at the end

annotation.surface: A husband pocketing some money on top of everything else.
annotation.walkthrough: The obvious pounds abbreviation is LB, but here it is the single L of £, which slips between TO and BOOT.
annotation.definitionFit: A booth beside the road where tolls are collected.

entries.clue: Cats, say, not usually considered this when yowling? (7)

annotation.definition: Cats, say, not usually considered this when yowling?

blocks.note: the surface wants real cats; the setter means Cats, the Lloyd Webber stage show

blocks.clueFragment: not usually considered this when yowling?
blocks.note: real cats yowling are not thought tuneful, so the adjective and the noun share one word

annotation.surface: A remark that caterwauling cats are not exactly tuneful.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer works twice: Cats is a musical, and yowling cats are anything but musical.
annotation.definitionFit: Cats is a stage musical, and a musical noise is a tuneful one.

entries.clue: What abbot would assume his back is covered in muck? (5)

indicatorNotes.back: a word's back is its end, so 'his back' is the last letter of abbot, whom 'his' refers to
indicatorNotes.is covered in: something covered in muck is wrapped by it, so T sits inside MIRE

blocks.note: the abbot's back: last letter of abboT, inside MIRE

annotation.surface: An abbot worried that he has sat down in the mud.
annotation.walkthrough: 'His' points back to the abbot, so his back is the T at the end of the word abbot, not the letter S of 'his'. 'Assume' means put on, as clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: The tall headdress worn by bishops and some abbots.

entries.clue: Lies from southern politicians (7)

annotation.surface: A jibe that politicians from the south are liars.
annotation.walkthrough: Tories are members of Britain's Conservative Party. 'Lies' looks like a verb but is the noun, matching STORIES.
annotation.definitionFit: Telling stories is a mild way of saying telling lies.

entries.clue: Fancy lay Catholic not in any order (11)

indicatorNotes.Fancy: fancy as in elaborate or fanciful: the letters are rearranged into a fancier form

annotation.surface: Musing on whether a lay Catholic belongs to any religious order.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface uses 'order' in its monastic sense, which is exactly why 'not in any order' reads as churchy rather than as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Done without any arrangement or sequence, in a jumble.

entries.clue: Philosopher under large blanket (5)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down answer, 'under' puts AYER physically below L

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A philosopher lying under a large blanket.
annotation.walkthrough: Blocks are listed top to bottom: the philosopher goes under L.
annotation.definitionFit: A blanket of snow or fog is a covering sheet of it.

entries.clue: Spin, then nothing followed in speech, getting spin out (8)

indicatorNotes.then: 'then' means next in sequence, so O follows PR
indicatorNotes.in speech: something said in speech is heard rather than read, so 'tracked' gives the sound TRACT

blocks.note: PR = public relations, which puts a spin on things
followed = tracked, which sounds like tract

annotation.surface: A political commentary on spin doctors, repeating the word spin twice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spin' appears twice with two jobs: first as PR, then inside the definition 'spin out', meaning prolong.
annotation.definitionFit: To draw something out in time, prolonging it.

entries.clue: Footballer who creates dramatic scenes? (9)

blocks.note: a real footballer: the answer is a football position
the surface suggests a player throwing tantrums; the setter means a maker of plays, and plays have scenes

annotation.surface: A footballer who throws theatrical tantrums on the pitch.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer read in two halves is a play-maker, a dramatist; as one word it is the player who sets up attacks.
annotation.definitionFit: The midfielder who sets up the team's attacking moves.

entries.clue: Missing the start, reports on spells in game (5)

indicatorNotes.Missing the start: a word missing its start has lost its first letter, so COVERS drops C

blocks.note: COVERS (as a journalist covers a story) without its C

annotation.surface: A journalist, having missed the opening, writes up passages of a game.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls from one bowler, so overs are spells within the game.
annotation.definitionFit: Cricket's successive six-ball spells of bowling.

entries.clue: Valiant suspect again? (11)

blocks.note: open to doubt, able to be suspected

annotation.surface: Asking whether a brave person is under suspicion once more.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is split whimsically as RE-DOUBTABLE, able to be doubted again; the real word has nothing to do with doubt.
annotation.definitionFit: Formidable, worthy of respect for courage.

entries.clue: My face is friendly (7)

blocks.note: cor! and my! are both exclamations of surprise

annotation.surface: Someone boasting that they have a friendly face.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' is not the possessive but the exclamation, as in 'My, how you've grown'. Cor is its British equivalent, and dial is slang for the face.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for warm and genial, from Latin cor, heart.

entries.clue: How for a while the French marked the turning of the year? (13,8)

annotation.definition: How for a while the French marked the turning of the year?

blocks.clueFragment: How for a while the French marked
blocks.note: a straight history question: the system France used for a few years
the surface means new year; the setter means a revolution, a turning, of the calendar

annotation.surface: A history question about how France celebrated the new year.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'turning of the year' plays on revolution as a turn; France's post-Revolution calendar ran from 1793 to 1805.
annotation.definitionFit: The calendar France adopted after the Revolution, in use for about twelve years.

entries.clue: Resolution to support band, but not with single (8)

indicatorNotes.but not: 'band, but not and' strips the letters AND out of band
indicatorNotes.with: 'with' means accompanied by, so ONE comes along after the B

blocks.note: BAND with AND removed: the clue's own 'and' is spelt out as the deleted letters

annotation.surface: A decision to back a group, but without releasing a single.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'band but not [and]': the word 'and' is taken out of band. It looks like a musical decision about singles and support acts.
annotation.definitionFit: Firmness of character, the figurative spine that keeps someone upright.

entries.clue: Temporary home schooling period across island (7)

indicatorNotes.across: something stretched across another spans it on both sides, so TERM reaches round I

annotation.surface: Temporary housing for a family during the school term on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temporary home' looks like a single phrase, but the definition stops at Temporary and 'home' is IN.
annotation.definitionFit: Provisional, holding good only for the time being.

entries.clue: Foolish and irrational to interrupt boss (6)

indicatorNotes.to interrupt: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so PI breaks into STUD

blocks.note: a stud or boss is a raised knob, as on a shield
pi is an irrational number, placed inside STUD

annotation.surface: An employee behaving foolishly and irrationally by cutting in on the boss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is not an employer but a round knob, a stud. 'Irrational' is the mathematical sense: pi cannot be written as a fraction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone lacking good sense.

entries.clue: Obviously highly amused, mutating this insect (2,8)

indicatorNotes.mutating: to mutate is to change form, so the letters of 'this insect' take a new arrangement

annotation.surface: Someone laughing at the sight of an insect changing its shape.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a science-fiction mutation, but 'mutating' just shuffles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: laughing so hard it gives you a stitch in your side.

entries.clue: Back-to-back opera and West End production share a founding standard (9)

indicatorNotes.Back-to-back: two things back to back face opposite ways, so EVITA is turned round to meet NORMA
indicatorNotes.share a: the two words overlap, using their letter A only once

blocks.note: the musical EVITA reversed is ATIVE; its A is the one shared with NORMA

annotation.surface: An opera and a West End show sharing the credit for establishing a standard.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue says it outright: 'share a' means the letter A is used once for both words. The West End is London's theatre district.
annotation.definitionFit: Establishing or relating to a norm, a standard to follow.

entries.clue: Talk tediously about old killer (7)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in its sense of around: HARP ON is placed around O

blocks.note: to harp on = to go on and on
O = old, placed inside HARP ON

annotation.surface: A bore droning on about a historic murderer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old killer' looks like a single noun phrase, a veteran murderer; 'old' is the O and the killer is the weapon.
annotation.definitionFit: The barbed spear used to kill whales.

entries.clue: Rhymes used by old-fashioned teacher? (5,3,4)

blocks.note: the surface suggests nursery rhymes; the setter means two words that rhyme with each other
the blackboard and the lecture, the tools of traditional teaching

annotation.surface: A teacher reciting nursery rhymes to a class.
annotation.walkthrough: The rhymes are the two halves of the answer, which is also the name for the traditional blackboard-and-lecture method.
annotation.definitionFit: The old style of teaching from the front at a blackboard.

entries.clue: Caught wearing extra habit (9)

indicatorNotes.wearing: clothing a person is wearing wraps round them, so ADDITION wraps round C

blocks.note: C = caught, cricket scoring, inside ADDITION

annotation.surface: A nun caught wearing a spare habit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Habit' plays on the nun's garment, which suits 'wearing'; the definition means a dependency.
annotation.definitionFit: Habit in its dependency sense, not the monk's robe the surface suggests.

entries.clue: Foolishness of many points surrounding love (8)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: to surround is to be on every side, so the string of points goes round O

blocks.note: a run of compass points: N, N, S, E, N, S, E
love = O, zero in tennis, inserted after the first N

annotation.surface: Complaining that an argument with many points about love is silly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Many points' is a loose instruction: the solver has to find a run of compass points that fits round the O.
annotation.definitionFit: Silly talk or behaviour lacking any sense.

entries.clue: Scottish bank’s asinine utterance picked up (4)

indicatorNotes.picked up: heard, as a microphone picks up a sound, so the spelling follows the sound

annotation.surface: A Scottish bank caught out making a stupid statement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Asinine' means stupid, which fits a bank's gaffe; literally it means donkey-like, and the donkey's cry is a bray.
annotation.definitionFit: A Scots word for a hillside or steep slope.

entries.clue: Englishman perhaps holding small light stood up (8)

indicatorNotes.holding: to hold something is to have it inside your grasp, so BRIT has S inside it

blocks.note: an Englishman is one kind of Brit

annotation.surface: An Englishman carrying a torch, getting to his feet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stood up' suggests a person rising; it is hairs on end.
annotation.definitionFit: Said of hair or fur rising on end, as on an angry cat's back.

entries.clue: Jackson’s display stand contains only second-hand things? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a possessive pointing at the name: Jackson's first name

indicatorNotes.contains: a stall that contains goods has them inside it, so STALL has O NEW inside

blocks.note: nothing new = O (nothing) + NEW, placed inside STALL

annotation.surface: A market stall run by a Jackson that sells only used goods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Only second-hand things' is a riddle for 'O NEW', nothing new. Stonewall Jackson was a Confederate general in the American Civil War.
annotation.definitionFit: Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson got his nickname at the First Battle of Bull Run.

entries.clue: Press bell and run away? One’s fixed with an eye (8)

annotation.surface: The childish prank of ringing a doorbell and running off.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is knock-down ginger, the prank of ringing and fleeing; the answer is hardware.
annotation.definitionFit: A bolt with an eye at its head, holding a ring.

entries.clue: Dissipating real gloom to take on major importance (4,5)

indicatorNotes.Dissipating: to dissipate is to scatter, as mist does, so the letters disperse and reform

annotation.surface: Gloom lifting only for something weightier to take its place.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder hides LOOM almost whole inside GLOOM, which helps once spotted.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that looms large becomes prominent and pressing.

entries.clue: Gradually overcome resistance of dress with feathers (4,4)

blocks.note: dress = wear, as in evening wear

annotation.surface: A persuasion scene where a feathered dress wins someone round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dress with feathers' reads as one garment, but the words split into two nouns.
annotation.definitionFit: To erode someone's opposition bit by bit.

entries.clue: Flawed company involved in wasted money — with this? (5,7)

annotation.definition: Flawed company involved in wasted money — with this?

indicatorNotes.involved in: something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so CO goes inside the reshuffled MONEY
indicatorNotes.wasted: wasted in its sense of ruined or wrecked: MONEY is broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: CO = company, inside ENOMY to make E-CO-NOMY

annotation.surface: A firm that ended up throwing money away by trying to save it.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: a company wasting money is the classic result of a false economy, which the final 'with this?' invites the solver to supply.
annotation.definitionFit: A saving that ends up costing more, which is how a company wastes money.

entries.clue: Spot extremely colourful animal? Yes and no, after reflection (4,4,2)

indicatorNotes.extremely: 'extremely' points at a word's extremes, its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.after reflection: a reflection in a mirror reverses left and right, so NO is read backwards

annotation.surface: Wondering whether one saw a gaudy creature, answering 'yes and no' after some thought.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' sounds like an evasive answer, but YES is used literally and only NO is reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom for catching sight of something.

entries.clue: A stammering king’s very attentive (3,4)

blocks.note: the stammer repeats the first letter of Lear
King Lear's, with the apostrophe dropped

annotation.surface: A king with a stutter who nonetheless listens carefully.
annotation.walkthrough: A stammer is shown by doubling a word's first letter: L-LEAR'S. The king is Shakespeare's Lear.
annotation.definitionFit: Listening with full attention, as if made of nothing but ears.

entries.clue: Ransack mountains where there is much shooting (5,5)

annotation.surface: Raiders plundering a mountain area full of gunfire.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the answer are the same words used in different senses, which the surface of raiders and gunfire hides.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a place set aside for target practice with guns.

entries.clue: Scurrying around, tolerates us idle folk (5-6)

indicatorNotes.Scurrying around: scurrying around is running here and there in disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order

annotation.surface: Busy people complaining that the lazy put up with them.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sets busy scurrying against idleness, the opposite of what the answer describes.
annotation.definitionFit: From the Odyssey, where eating the lotus left men in dreamy indolence.

entries.clue: Hesitate as stupid woman putting in hour with each son (6-6)

indicatorNotes.putting in: to put something in is to insert it, so an H goes into each of the two words

blocks.note: H = hour, once for each word
S = son: each H goes in beside an S, the first letter of SILLY and of SALLY

annotation.surface: Someone dithering like a foolish woman who fusses over an hour with each of her sons.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With each son' tells you where the H goes: alongside the S at the start of each word, so both words change the same way.
annotation.definitionFit: A reduplicated idiom for dithering, from 'shall I, shall I'.

entries.clue: Assistant’s service trimming top in hairdresser’s (11)

indicatorNotes.trimming top: a trim takes a little off the top, so VESPERS loses its first letter
indicatorNotes.in: 'in hairdresser's' places ESPERS within SALON, like a customer in the shop

blocks.note: VESPERS, the evening church service, without V, inside SALON

annotation.surface: A hairdresser's assistant giving a customer a trim.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests the salon's service to customers; it is the church service of vespers. The 's after Assistant stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: In British usage a shop assistant is the person who serves customers and sells.

entries.clue: In wild anger, lashes loss of spirit (6,5)

indicatorNotes.wild: wild in its sense of uncontrolled: the letters of 'anger, lashes' run free into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone lashing out in rage and losing heart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loss of spirit' reads as despondency; it means whisky or brandy lost to evaporation while it ages in the cask.
annotation.definitionFit: The spirit that evaporates from the barrel during maturation, taken by the angels.

entries.clue: American can relax, given space (4,4)

annotation.surface: An American who can finally put their feet up with room to spare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb but is the noun, US slang for a toilet; a restroom is the American word for a public lavatory.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are American terms for a toilet, one polite and one slang.

entries.clue: Two months suggested? Perhaps June and July (9)

indicatorNotes.suggested: the answer only suggests the two months, as a clue suggests its solution: take its first half as an instruction and it produces them

blocks.note: MM: M is the abbreviation for month, so two months are M and M
the answer, split in two, is an instruction to take the middle of a word, and that middle is MM

annotation.surface: Guessing which two months are meant, with June and July offered as an example.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'mid summer': the middle letters of SUMMER are MM, and M is the abbreviation for month. The second half gives the plain sense.
annotation.definitionFit: June and July sit in the middle of the northern summer.

entries.clue: Yearn to enter a crack corps? Provided (2,4,2)

indicatorNotes.to enter: to enter a regiment is to join it, going inside, so LONG goes inside SAS

blocks.note: the SAS, the British special forces regiment
to long = to yearn, placed inside SAS

annotation.surface: Someone longing to join an elite unit, on one condition.
annotation.walkthrough: The SAS is the British Army's Special Air Service. 'Provided' is not a past tense here but the conditional, as in 'provided you pay'.
annotation.definitionFit: Both introduce a condition: provided that, so long as.

entries.clue: Travel by railway is bloody (4)

annotation.surface: A grumble that rail travel is a bloody nuisance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads as a British swear word, but the definition means covered in blood.
annotation.definitionFit: Full of bloodshed, the literal sense of the word.

entries.clue: We hear payment method ready for use, here? (8)

annotation.definition: We hear payment method ready for use, here?

indicatorNotes.We hear: what we hear is a sound, not a spelling, so 'cheque' can be written CHECK

blocks.note: a cheque, spelt the American way when heard
out = available, as a new product is out

annotation.surface: A shopper asking about payment at the till.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, with 'here?' pointing to where you pay; the wordplay runs across it.
annotation.definitionFit: The till in a shop, which is where a cheque would be ready for use.

entries.clue: Show where Detroit and Adelaide are closely linked? (4,3,5)

annotation.definition: Show where Detroit and Adelaide are closely linked?

blocks.note: the surface suggests 'demonstrate'; the setter means a stage show

blocks.clueFragment: where Detroit and Adelaide are closely linked?
blocks.note: not two cities on different continents but Nathan Detroit and Miss Adelaide, a long-engaged couple

annotation.surface: A geography puzzle about two cities on different continents.
annotation.walkthrough: Detroit and Adelaide look like cities; they are characters in a Broadway musical, engaged for fourteen years.
annotation.definitionFit: The Loesser musical in which Nathan Detroit and Adelaide are engaged.

entries.clue: Perhaps missed church to get a divorce? (7)

annotation.surface: Wondering whether skipping church is grounds for divorce.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Missed church' reads as skipping the service; 'missed' is UNHIT, and getting hitched means marrying.
annotation.definitionFit: Since getting hitched is marrying, undoing the hitch is jokingly divorcing.

entries.clue: Be ruthless, smashing public convenience (3,7)

indicatorNotes.smashing: something smashed is broken into pieces, so the letters of 'be ruthless' are broken up and reassembled

annotation.surface: A vandal told to be ruthless in wrecking a public toilet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Public convenience' is the British euphemism for a public toilet; here it means a facility that is convenient for the public.
annotation.definitionFit: A roadside shelter is a public amenity, a convenience in the literal sense.

entries.clue: Buffet is full of eats, principally sandwiches (7)

indicatorNotes.full of: something full of E has E inside it, so IS holds E
indicatorNotes.principally: 'principally' means first and foremost, so only the first letter of 'eats' is used

blocks.note: to buffet or butt = to strike
the first letter of eats, inside IS

annotation.surface: A buffet table laden with food, mostly sandwiches.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' reads as a spread of food but is the verb to strike.
annotation.definitionFit: Northern English slang, as in a chip or bacon butty.

entries.clue: Actor finally entering stage for a few words (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: 'finally' means at the end, so only the last letter of actor is used
indicatorNotes.entering: an actor entering a stage walks into it, so R goes inside PHASE

blocks.note: last letter of actoR, inside PHASE

annotation.surface: An actor at last stepping on stage to deliver a short line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stage' is set up as a theatre stage for the actor; it means a phase.
annotation.definitionFit: A short sequence forming a unit of meaning, less than a full sentence.

entries.clue: William Brown’s sister bore the lined curtains off (5)

indicatorNotes.curtains off: strip away the surrounding letters, the curtains, to reveal the answer inside

annotation.surface: A girl from a children's book wearing a dress whose lining she has removed.
annotation.walkthrough: William Brown is the unruly boy in Richmal Crompton's Just William stories, much loved in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: William's glamorous older sister in the Just William books.

entries.clue: Cried beside us in Vienna, perhaps still harbouring bugs (7)

indicatorNotes.beside: 'beside' means next to, so WEPT is placed alongside UNS

blocks.note: uns is German for us, spoken in Vienna

annotation.surface: Someone weeping in Vienna, perhaps with a cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' suggests germs; it means hidden microphones, and a room not yet swept for them may still hold them.
annotation.definitionFit: A room not yet checked for listening devices may still contain them.

entries.clue: Almost secure someone else’s place? (5)

indicatorNotes.Almost: almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

annotation.surface: Nearly getting a secure position that belongs to someone else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Secure' reads as a verb, to obtain; it is the adjective steady, firm.
annotation.definitionFit: To act in someone's stead is to stand in for them.

entries.clue: Abandon playwright for worthless piece (8)

blocks.note: to kick a habit = to abandon it

annotation.surface: Advice to drop a dramatist in favour of a trivial work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a play, fitting the playwright; a kickshaw is a trinket or a fancy dish.
annotation.definitionFit: A trifle or bauble, from French quelque chose, 'something'.

entries.clue: First person on the water, taking key, vacated outside pool (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down answer, 'on' puts I on top of TT
indicatorNotes.taking: taking in its sense of taking on board: the key is brought into the assembly
indicatorNotes.vacated: a vacated house is emptied, so KEY loses its middle, leaving KY
indicatorNotes.outside: 'outside' in its positional sense: K and Y stand on either side of ITT

blocks.note: KeY with its inside removed; its K and Y go round the rest
someone on the water is teetotal, TT

annotation.surface: The first person out on the water taking a key before heading out to a pool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the water' means drinking only water, TT for teetotal. I on TT makes ITT, then the emptied key wraps round it.
annotation.definitionFit: A shared fund that players or colleagues pay into, as in a card game.

entries.clue: So far unknown in a group (2,3)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in a group' means being a member, inside it, so Y goes inside A SET

blocks.note: y, an unknown in algebra, inside A SET

annotation.surface: A member of a group whose identity is not yet known.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unknown' is the algebraic unknown; x, y and z all serve.
annotation.definitionFit: Until now, up to the present time.

entries.clue: Where to look up barrister? (3,8,10)

blocks.note: the surface means where to go and find someone; the setter means where to look up a word
barristers work from chambers, which is also the name of the dictionary

annotation.surface: Asking where to find a lawyer.
annotation.walkthrough: A barrister is found in chambers, the set of offices barristers share; the answer is the dictionary most used by crossword setters.
annotation.definitionFit: A reference book in which any word, barrister included, can be looked up.

entries.clue: Artist and what he may wet with touch of red (8)

indicatorNotes.touch of: a touch is a small amount, so only the first letter of red

blocks.note: to wet one's whistle = to have a drink

annotation.surface: A painter with a glass of red wine in hand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Touch of red' is set up as a painter's dab of colour; with 'wet' it also suggests red wine.
annotation.definitionFit: James McNeill Whistler painted Whistler's Mother.

entries.clue: Powerful family departs, some upset by scene of squalor (7)

indicatorNotes.upset: to upset is to knock over, so ANY is turned back to front

blocks.note: a pigsty is a byword for filth

annotation.surface: A grand family leaving, some of them upset by the squalid surroundings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as distressed; it is the reversal instruction on 'some'.
annotation.definitionFit: A succession of rulers or magnates from one line, as the Tudors or Kennedys.

entries.clue: Agreement that others will pay for years (6)

blocks.note: if something is your treat, you pay for others

annotation.surface: A deal where someone else foots the bill for years.
annotation.walkthrough: A treat is something paid for by someone else, so the long phrase stands for one short word.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal pact between states, the diplomatic sense.
